title: Englewood, Colorado well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: In Englewood, Colorado, most wells are about 31 ft deep with a typical 13.8 gpm yield. Here’s what that means for drilling cost and water supply.
h1: Understanding water wells around Englewood, Colorado
intro_html:
Englewood sits over the Denver Basin, with a mix of shallow alluvial wells and very deep bedrock completions. The state has records for 7,552 well permits within about 5 miles, so we have a decent picture of what to expect for depth, yield, and cost between Sheridan, Cherry Hills Village, Bow Mar, Columbine Valley, Holly Hills, and Littleton.

If you’re buying a home on a well or planning new construction, pay attention to the big spread in depths here, the strong but variable yields, and the number of monitoring wells tied to local contamination work.

sections.heading: How deep wells run in Englewood
sections.html:
Most recorded wells around Englewood are quite shallow, but there’s a long tail of very deep holes. The median total depth is only 31 feet, and the middle half of wells fall between 21 and 57 feet. About 82% of wells are under 100 feet.

That said, 9% of wells go deeper than 600 feet, the 90th percentile depth jumps to 490 feet, and the deepest well on record reaches 2,200 feet. Those deeper completions are typically into Denver Basin bedrock, often for municipal or monitoring purposes, not just a single home.

For a new household well, a driller will usually bid based on this range: budget for a shallow alluvial well but be aware that a deep Denver aquifer well is possible on some sites.

sections.heading: Well yield and how much water you can expect
sections.html:
Where wells do get completed for use around Englewood, they tend to be productive. Reported pump yields have a median of 13.8 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 9.0 and 16.8 gpm. That’s more than enough for a typical household, small lawn, and normal indoor use.

The low-yield risk is present but not extreme. About 3% of tested wells make under 1 gpm, and 11% fall between 1 and 5 gpm. On the strong side, 41% are in the 5–15 gpm band and 45% report 15+ gpm.

This spread means you should still check neighboring well records before buying, but in general the area is not known for chronic low-production domestic wells.

sections.heading: Water levels and long‑term trend near Englewood
sections.html:
Static water levels reported around Englewood are generally shallow. The overall median depth to water is 15 feet, with the middle half of measurements between 11 and 26 feet below the surface. That’s consistent with a mix of alluvial and shallow bedrock sources near the South Platte corridor and surrounding developments.

The long-term data do not show a simple steady decline. Median static levels were about 30 feet in the 1950s and 45 feet in the 1960s, then much shallower in recent decades: about 16 feet in the 2010s and 13 feet in the 2020s. That suggests local conditions, recharge, and changes in what kinds of wells are being measured have kept water tables from dropping off sharply in this immediate area.

sections.heading: Who is drilling here and how activity has changed
sections.html:
Englewood’s well history is busy and fairly modern. Within 5 miles, permits per decade ramped up from 188 in the 1950s and 162 in the 1960s to 282 in the 1970s and 284 in the 1980s. Activity then jumped sharply: 1,832 permits in the 1990s and 2,080 in the 2000s, with 814 in the 2010s and 452 so far in the 2020s. The newest permits run through 2025.

About 60% of these are monitoring wells, not household supplies, which fits with the number of environmental cleanup projects in and around Englewood. The most active drillers on record are Authorized (Pe, Pg) with 3,091 wells, Hier Drilling Co Inc (Hier, Bruce A.) with 236, and Ground Exploration LLC (Bender, Joseph T.) with 113.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost in Englewood
sections.html:
The ground here is Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock with local alluvium, and the cost model reflects that. Typical drilling rates run about $50–$70 per foot. At the local median depth of 31 feet, the drilled hole alone works out around $1,600–$2,200.

Once you add pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, a completed well at that median depth usually lands in the $7,600–$14,200 range. If your site ends up needing a few hundred feet of bedrock drilling instead of a shallow well, those per-foot costs multiply quickly.

When you bid a new well, have the driller price both a shallow scenario and a deeper Denver Basin scenario so you’re not surprised if they have to keep going.

sections.heading: Contamination, low-yield, and other risks to check
sections.html:
Englewood is heavily studied for environmental issues. Within about 10 miles there are 492 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 27 historic mine features, and 153 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That lines up with the high share of monitoring wells, and it means water quality is a real consideration.

Before you rely on a private well, review nearby monitoring data, test for PFAS and common urban contaminants, and pay attention to any plumes that may affect your aquifer. On the supply side, only 3% of tested wells are under 1 gpm, but those do exist, so don’t skip a pump test if you’re buying.

Also coordinate well and septic locations carefully so setbacks are met and your leach field does not impact your own water source.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a lot around Englewood
sections.html:
For a lot in Englewood, Sheridan, Cherry Hills Village, or the nearby small communities, start by pulling the Colorado DWR well permits within a mile or two. Look at total depths, yields, and static levels, not just the nearest single well.

Keep in mind that 100% of wells are classified to Denver Basin aquifers, but many are shallow compared to the big regional supply wells. Confirm whether your future well will likely be alluvial and shallow or a deeper bedrock completion, because that drives cost and long-term reliability.

In this area, also take the contamination mapping seriously. Between the PFAS sites and other cleanup projects, factor in robust water testing as part of due diligence before closing on land or starting construction.

faq.q: How deep are water wells around Englewood, Colorado?
faq.a: Around Englewood, the median well depth on record is 31 feet, with the middle half between 21 and 57 feet. About 82% of wells are under 100 feet, but there’s a long tail: 4% run 100–300 feet, 5% are 300–600 feet, and 9% go deeper than 600 feet. The deepest well in the records reaches 2,200 feet.

faq.q: How much water do Englewood wells usually produce?
faq.a: Reported pump yields near Englewood have a median of 13.8 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 9.0 and 16.8 gpm. Only about 3% of wells report less than 1 gpm and 11% are between 1 and 5 gpm, while 41% fall in the 5–15 gpm range and 45% report more than 15 gpm, which is strong for domestic use.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Englewood, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety depends on the specific well. Within about 10 miles of Englewood there are 492 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 153 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, so water quality needs to be checked carefully. Many wells are monitoring wells tied to these issues. For any private supply well, plan on full lab testing, including PFAS, before relying on it for drinking water.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a water well in Englewood?
faq.a: In the Englewood area, drilling through Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock typically runs $50–$70 per foot. At the local median depth of 31 feet, that puts the borehole itself around $1,600–$2,200. A fully finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical usually totals about $7,600–$14,200 at that depth, with deeper wells costing proportionally more.

faq.q: Are water levels dropping around Englewood?
faq.a: Available static water level data don’t show a simple long-term decline. The overall median depth to water is about 15 feet, with most readings between 11 and 26 feet. By decade, medians were around 30 feet in the 1950s, 45 feet in the 1960s, then much shallower in recent years: about 16 feet in the 2010s and 13 feet in the 2020s. That suggests no clear local drop in the recent record.
